---
title: "Reading the Family and Fertility Surveys (FFS)"
---

The Family and Fertility Surveys (FFS, 1990s) come as fixed-width text with SPSS syntax, not as Stata or SPSS
files. Every country's archive holds three files:

| file | what it is |
|---|---|
| `COUNTRY.DAT` | the data: fixed-width text, 44 to 83 lines per respondent depending on the country |
| `COUNTRY.SPS` | SPSS syntax that reads it: `DATA LIST` (record and columns of each variable), `VARIABLE LABELS`, `VALUE LABELS`, `MISSING VALUE` |
| `COUNTRY.TBL` | the published frequency tables, to check results against; not needed to read the data |

Estonia ships ready-made `.SAV` files instead of a `.SPS`; Greece has no `.TBL` and its `.SPS` has no labels.

## Download and conversion

```bash
ggp-client download   --project ffs --country at     # raw files, plus converted_data.dta
ggp-client download   --project ffs --ext sav        # converted to sav instead
ggp-client preprocess --project ffs                  # parquet + meta.json from the converted file
```

```
data/download/raw/ffs/at/ffs_at.dat                    the raw files, renamed after the dataset
data/download/raw/ffs/at/ffs_at.sps
data/download/raw/ffs/at/ffs_at.tbl
data/download/processed/ffs/at/converted_data.dta      converted, with variable and value labels
data/download/processed/ffs/at/converted_data.parquet  after preprocess
data/download/processed/ffs/at/converted_data.meta.json
```

FFS converts to `.dta` (default) or `.sav`, the formats that hold labels. Estonia has two samples and a total, so
its names get the sample added (`ffs_ee_est_f.dat`, `converted_data_est_f.dta`). One dataset by hand, outside the
catalogue: `ggp-client convert AUSTRIA.SPS --ext dta sav`.

What the conversion does:

- Every `$` in a variable name becomes `_`, as Stata does not allow `$`: `IND01$01` is `IND01_01`. The raw `.sps`
  and `.tbl` are rewritten the same way on download (a `$` in a quoted label, or one outside a name such as
  `US$ 100`, stays), so syntax, tables and converted files use the same names.
- Missing-value codes such as 98 stay in the data and are labelled; `.sav` also marks them missing, as SPSS would.
- A cell that is not a number (the files use `*` for overflow) is read as missing, as SPSS does, and logged.
- The parser copes with the quirks of the real files: stray quotes where an umlaut was lost
  (`"Nieder"sterreich"`), text columns marked `(A)`, and labels shared by several variables.

## In SPSS

The raw files work directly. Open `ffs_at.sps`: its first line already reads `FILE='ffs_at.dat'` (the original
pointed at `C:\ISSA\...\AUSTRIA.DAT`). Make that the full path if SPSS does not find the file, add
`SAVE OUTFILE='ffs_at.sav'.` at the end, and run all.

## In R

R has no reader for SPSS syntax, so read the converted file with haven:

```r
library(haven)
ffs <- read_dta("data/download/processed/ffs/at/converted_data.dta")
table(as_factor(ffs$RESID))      # value labels as factor levels
attr(ffs$V917, "label")          # "Religion respondent"
```

With `--ext sav`, `read_sav(..., user_na = TRUE)` also keeps 98 and the like as labelled missing values.

## In Python

```python
from ggp_client import read
df = read.read("data/download/processed/ffs/at/converted_data.dta")   # polars DataFrame
df = read.read("data/download/raw/ffs/at/ffs_at.sps")                 # or straight from the raw files
```
